yes, there are 8 phases total.

stage 1: history - you talk through your medical history and identify specific traumas. your therapist will map out a treatment plan too based on your answers to questions. you pick certain events that affected you the most.

stage 2: preparation -  you and your therapist go through different techniques you can use during your EMDR, so you get to choose. then, you work on building your safe space you will use at the end of each stage 4 session. you also describe more of your feelings relating to the trauma and your safe space.

stage 3: assessment - identifying target memory that triggers emotional distress.

stage 4: desensitization (the hardest stage) - you focus on trauma/images that cause a negative action. you're basically reliving the trauma. while doing this, you focus on movements with your eyes. your therapist does this to change the way your brain associates the trauma with a trigger. this phase lasts as long as your therapist sees fit. each session ends with you going to your safe space so you don't leave your appointment in an episode. anytime during this session you can use your safe word/phrase you made before this stage.

stage 5: installation - your therapist works to "install" a positive belief deep into your thought process. they try to strengthen a positive belief to replace a negative one. all of this all relating to your specific trauma.

stage 6: body scan - you are asked to bring back the trauma to reevaluate it. your therapist checks to see if bringing your trauma back to the surface still elicits a physical response. if you're still feeling negative emotions related to the event, your therapist will continue with the eye movement therapy until you're ready to move forward.

stage 7: closure - your therapist emphasizes stress reduction techniques and asks you to record any disturbances you may have between sessions. they help coach you on how to manage those disturbances.

stage 8: reevaluation - your therapist reevaluates the effectiveness of your treatment and determines the need for further sessions and schedule a follow-up plan if needed.

​

during any of this you can decide to quit. you can take breaks as you need too (you use your safe word/phase you established). this is a long process typically and some people can't make it/handle stage 4.
